title: Linear local object cleanup pagination

requirements.LOP01: Replace quadratic directory-offset pagination with a designed and implemented linear complete scan.
requirements.LOP02: Retain durable continuation, bounded page memory/work, publication pins, reference protection and active-upload guards.
requirements.LOP03: Measure the original and final algorithms, preserve backup/restore, and record actual validation and limits.

outcome: Implemented in local source. One streaming manifest preparation, followed by direct byte-offset page reads. A 100000-object synthetic shard requires 100000 directory advances instead of the saved original's 5150000. No deployment or live cleanup was performed.

design.choice: Immutable disk-backed name manifest, not a new authoritative inventory or an in-memory directory iterator.
design.reason: A portable directory offset requires reopening and skipping the prefix. An in-memory iterator does not survive the maintenance CLI restarting between batches. A maintained database inventory would add coordination to uploads and need legacy/orphan reconciliation. A sequential manifest avoids those tradeoffs while leaving publication paths intact.
design.preparation: A fresh scan enumerates the existing 256 hash directories once, validates candidate names and regular-file entries, and appends shard/name records to a private .pending manifest. It fsyncs and atomically publishes a .scan file. Preparation is outside all maintenance database transactions and connections.

cursor.scan: 128-bit random scan ID local to the object root
cursor.offset: byte position at the next manifest record

design.paging: Seek directly to the byte offset. Consume at most the requested 1-1000 records, reread each current object's regular-file type, mtime and size, and skip missing files. No directory prefix is traversed. A candidate deletion cannot alter a manifest offset. No long-lived scan handles or population-sized Python collections are retained.
design.deletion: The manifest is only a candidate source. Existing current-reference checks, online publication pins, one-day age guard, offline-writer requirement, temporary guard locks and backup pause remain authoritative. Pending publication documents and proofs remain protected.
design.concurrency: An OS-released nonblocking builder lock permits one preparation at a time per root. Other processes can read existing manifests without acquiring the builder lock. Interrupted preparation leaves no usable partial cursor; retry cleans leftover private pending artifacts and rebuilds. Concurrent directory changes can wait for a later scan.
design.lifetime: At most four unfinished scans per volume. Manifests expire seven days after preparation. Completion creates a reclamation hint; the final page remains retryable until a fresh scan removes completed artifacts. Missing/expired cursors fail explicitly and must restart without a cursor. Reclamation touches only recognized regular scan artifacts, not object data or unknown files.
design.compatibility: Legacy {shard,offset} cursors restart once from the beginning without skipping a prefix. Objects may be rechecked safely. Retention no longer subtracts deleted-directory entries from the cursor. GCS/S3 adapters and existing content-addressed paths are unchanged.
design.startup: Constructor recovery keeps its separate 1000-directory-entry cap and never prepares a full manifest.
design.backup: Portable local archives prune .object-scans-v1 before descent. Rebuildable maintenance artifacts never enter an object archive. A symbolic link at the metadata-directory path is rejected. Real archive/restore and corruption/link checks pass.

complexity_and_resources.notation: N is the total directory entries visited; M is valid candidate names, M <= N; k is the page size, 1 <= k <= 1000.
complexity_and_resources.before: For N objects in a shard, a complete fixed-page scan advanced O(N^2/k) entries because each page reopened scandir and skipped its previous offset.
complexity_and_resources.after: One O(N) directory preparation pass, O(M) sequential manifest writes/reads, then O(k) work per page with direct byte seeks. A complete normal scan is O(N), with O(k) application memory. This counts work, not a promise about filesystem latency.
complexity_and_resources.disk: An ordinary object name record takes 73 bytes plus the 25-byte manifest header: 7,300,025 bytes for 100000 objects. Up to four unfinished scans can coexist. Temporary-file records have a different bounded length.
complexity_and_resources.tradeoff: The first scan preparation is deliberately O(N), not a bounded first-page latency. It needs temporary disk and may take time on a large NAS. It does not hold a DB connection or run during API startup. Interrupted preparation restarts its single enumeration rather than resuming a filesystem iterator.
complexity_and_resources.expiry: A scan must finish within seven days. A completed cursor can expire when a fresh scan begins. Start a new scan after completion; preserve and reuse the returned cursor during an active scan.

initial_corrections: Two initial patch attempts had context mismatches and made no partial changes; the storage method was then replaced against the verified current source.

Concurrent unrelated migration edits briefly caused a missing down_revision and then multiple schema heads. Storage-only tests passed independently. The initial mixed focused run had 32 passes and two migration setup errors; its XML is retained.

A disposable package snapshot was prepared for retention checks. Its setup assertion expected two migration heads, but concurrent edits had already joined them into one; no synthetic merge was written. The ensuing isolated check passed 37 tests with one PostgreSQL-dependent skip. The final actual workspace rerun passed all 74 selected tests and supersedes the workaround. No source migrations or existing assertions were changed.
WSL's read-only Python version probe returned E_ACCESSDENIED. No Linux execution, container operation or privilege escalation was performed.
